title: Ecclesiology and Bonhoeffer's Costly Discipleship
welcome_lead: Walk from John Paul II's Vatican to Dietrich Bonhoeffer's prison cell at Tegel as we study the Church and the cost of being its disciple.
meta_desc: A-Level Religious Studies adventure on ecclesiology and discipleship: marks of the Church, John Paul II's social teaching, and Bonhoeffer's Cost of Discipleship.
final_note: You have followed the Church from creedal marks to the radical demands of following the crucified Christ.

walkthroughs.h2: John Paul II and the Dignity of Work
walkthroughs.body_html: Karol Wojtyla's encyclical Laborem Exercens (1981) places the human person at the centre of work: work is for humans, not humans for work. Centesimus Annus (1991), marking the centenary of Rerum Novarum, criticised both Marxism and unfettered capitalism. Evangelium Vitae (1995) defended the 'culture of life' against abortion and euthanasia. His personalism rooted ethics in the imago Dei.

In The Cost of Discipleship (1937), Bonhoeffer opens with the searing distinction: 'Cheap grace is the deadly enemy of our Church. Costly grace is the treasure hidden in the field.' He read the Sermon on the Mount as a concrete call to obedience, not as an ideal. 'When Christ calls a man, he bids him come and die.'

Bonhoeffer co-founded the Confessing Church against Nazi Gleichschaltung and helped run the underground seminary at Finkenwalde. Arrested for his role in the conspiracy against Hitler, he was executed at Flossenburg in April 1945. His Letters and Papers from Prison introduced 'religionless Christianity' for 'a world come of age', anticipating later secular theology.

mcqs.q: What was the Augustine vs Pelagius dispute about original sin?
options: Augustine argued humans inherit a corrupted nature from Adam (original sin) and cannot achieve salvation without grace; Pelagius argued humans retain free will to choose good without divine intervention and that sin is imitated, not inherited.
The Trinity refers to heaven, earth and hell.
Original sin means Christians believe babies are evil.
Pelagius and Augustine agreed humans are born innocent.
